title: A solid can be stored as its skin, as a distance field, or as a grid, and each makes different operations easy
summary: A CAD kernel stores the boundary of a solid as faces, edges and vertices. A signed distance function stores the distance to the boundary at every point, which turns Boolean operations into min and max. Meshing then fills the solid with simple cells whose shape decides how good a simulation can be.

read_the_figure.question: Is the mesh fine where the solution changes fast, smooth where it does not, and made of well-shaped cells?
read_the_figure.axes: There are no data axes: the left panel shows the full mesh around the body, the right a zoom at the wall. The annotation gives the first cell height as a fraction of the diameter and the growth ratio between successive layers.
look_at: Where the lines crowd together: that is where the mesh is fine, and it should be where gradients are large (here at the wall).
Growth of the cell size away from the wall: a ratio of about 1.2 to 1.5 is smooth, a sudden jump is a quality problem.
The shape of the cells: near-square cells are good, long thin ones are only acceptable when aligned with the flow.
The first-cell height against the physics that the wall layer needs resolved, stated in the annotation.
read_the_figure.proves: A mesh that is graded smoothly with well-shaped cells is necessary for an accurate solution. It is not sufficient: only a grid-convergence study shows the solution no longer depends on it.
if_wrong: Abrupt jumps in cell size, or cells with a very large or very small angle: interpolation error rises and the solver can converge slowly or fail.
A first cell far thicker than the layer it should resolve: the near-wall gradient is not captured.
A mesh that looks beautiful but was never refined: nothing here shows grid independence.
must_check: Both a full view and a zoom at the region that matters.
First-cell height, growth ratio and number of cells stated.
A quality measure reported (minimum angle, aspect ratio or skewness).
The geometry representation the mesh was built from named.

terms.meaning: A solid described by its skin: faces (surface patches), the edges where they meet and the vertices where edges meet, plus how they are connected.
Topology is the connectivity (which face touches which edge). Geometry is the shape (the equation of the surface). A B-rep needs both and they must agree.
A function that gives the distance from a point to the surface, negative inside and positive outside.
The set of points where a function takes one value. The surface of an SDF solid is its zero level set.
A solid stored as inside or outside on a regular 3D lattice of cells.
Sweeping a 2D profile along a line or around an axis to make a solid.
A rounded blend that replaces a sharp edge by a surface of constant radius.
Union, intersection and difference of solids.
The triangulation of a point set in which no point lies inside the circumscribed circle of any triangle.
The region of space that is closer to one point than to any other. The Voronoi diagram is the dual of the Delaunay triangulation.
A number that says how close a cell is to its ideal shape, such as an equilateral triangle.

remember: B-rep stores faces, edges and vertices plus connectivity. For a closed surface of genus $g$, $V-E+F=2(1-g)$.
Union $=\min$, intersection $=\max$, difference $=\max(a,-b)$. Exact on one side only.
Smooth min $-k\ln(e^{-a/k}+e^{-b/k})$ rounds the crease and tends to min as $k\to0$.
Delaunay: empty circumcircle, $T=2n-2-h$ triangles. Quality $q=4\sqrt3A/(a^2+b^2+c^2)$, 1 is equilateral.

understand.title: Intuition
understand.text: Think of a mug. You can describe it by its skin (the inner and outer cylinder, the bottom, the handle, and how they join): that is a B-rep, precise and editable, with exact curved surfaces. You can describe it by a function that tells you, from any point in the room, how far you are from the mug: that is an SDF, and asking whether a point is inside is just checking a sign. Or you can describe it as a pile of tiny cubes. Each representation answers different questions cheaply.

understand.title: What each is good for
understand.text: B-rep is what CAD uses, because it keeps exact surfaces, edges you can select, and a history of features. Its difficulty is the Boolean operation: two surfaces must be intersected exactly and the topology rebuilt. SDFs make unions and intersections trivial and blends smooth, so they are popular for implicit modelling and for shape optimisation, but you must extract a surface (marching cubes) to mesh or manufacture. Voxels are simplest and what image-based simulation uses, but they carry staircase error.

understand.title: The hard tier
understand.text: Min and max of exact distance functions are only exact on one side of the surface: the union is exact outside and the intersection exact inside, so the result is a bound rather than a distance in the other region. Algorithms that need a true distance (offsets, filleting, ray-marching with large steps) must reinitialise the field. B-rep Booleans are hard for the opposite reason: tolerances. Two faces that should meet along an edge differ by a tiny gap, and a kernel must decide whether that is the same edge. Robust kernels spend most of their code on that.

steps.title: Three ways to store a solid
steps.note: The B-rep keeps the boundary exactly, the SDF keeps a field whose sign gives the solid, the voxel grid keeps a mask.

steps.title: A valid closed B-rep obeys an Euler formula
steps.note: A cube: $8-12+6=2$, genus 0. A torus built from a quad grid, for example $16-32+16=0$, genus 1. Checking this after a kernel operation catches a broken shell. Verified by counting on both shapes.

steps.title: Extrude and revolve give volumes immediately
steps.note: The torus preset sweeps a disc of radius 1 whose centre is at distance 3 from the axis, so $V=2\pi\cdot3\cdot\pi=6\pi^2$; integrating the shell form symbolically gives the same value.

steps.title: The simplest SDF: a sphere, and why the gradient has length one
steps.tex: f(\mathbf p)=\|\mathbf p\|-R,\qquad \|\nabla f\|=1,\qquad \mathbf n=\nabla f
steps.note: Verified symbolically. A true distance field has unit gradient (the eikonal equation), and its gradient on the surface is the outward normal. Many shapes have a closed form, such as the box below.

steps.title: A box, and the Boolean algebra of SDFs
steps.tex: \mathbf q=|\mathbf p|-\mathbf b,\quad f_\mathrm{box}=\|\max(\mathbf q,0)\|+\min(\max(q_x,q_y,q_z),0);\qquad f_{A\cup B}=\min(f_A,f_B),\ \ f_{A\cap B}=\max(f_A,f_B),\ \ f_{A\setminus B}=\max(f_A,-f_B)
steps.note: The box formula was compared with a brute-force distance to a dense sampling of the surface (agreement to sampling error). Union is a minimum because you are inside if you are inside either; intersection a maximum; difference intersects with the complement.

steps.title: What min and max do not give you
steps.tex: \text{union: exact outside, only }|f|\le d\text{ inside};\qquad \text{intersection: exact inside, only a bound outside}
steps.note: Checked with two overlapping discs against a dense boundary sample: outside both, the minimum equals the true distance to the union to 1e-9; inside the overlap it can be up to about 0.2 smaller in magnitude. The zero level set, which is the surface, is exact either way.

steps.title: Smooth union: a fillet in the field
steps.note: The limit and the value at $a=b$ are computed symbolically: the blend lowers the field exactly at the crease, where the two shapes meet, and by nothing far from it. A rounded box is the same idea in another form: a box with half-sizes reduced by $r$, offset by $r$, so $f=f_\mathrm{box}(\mathbf b-r)-r$ has corner radius $r$. Checked: the corner point of the inner box lies exactly $r$ from the surface along the diagonal.

steps.title: Delaunay triangulation and its dual
steps.tex: \text{no point inside any circumcircle},\qquad T=2n-2-h\ \ (n\text{ points},\ h\text{ on the convex hull})
steps.note: Checked on 60 random points: every triangle's circumcircle was empty and the count was 105 = 2*60 - 2 - 13. In 2D the Delaunay triangulation maximises the smallest angle among all triangulations of the same points, which is why it is the default for meshing. Its dual is the Voronoi diagram.

steps.title: Is the cell any good?
steps.note: Computed for an equilateral triangle (1.00), a right isosceles one (0.87) and a sliver 1 long and 0.05 high (0.12). Interpolation error grows as angles become large, so a mesh needs a minimum of $q$ and no sudden size jumps, in addition to a grid-convergence study.

worked.title: The volume of two overlapping spheres from their distance functions
worked.problem: Two unit spheres have centres 1 apart. Use the SDF union $f=\min(f_1,f_2)$ to find the volume of the union, analytically and by sampling the field on a grid.

solution.text: The overlap is two spherical caps of height $h=R-d/2=\tfrac12$.
Inclusion and exclusion: the union counts the lens once.
By sampling: count the grid cells where $\min(f_1,f_2)<0$ and multiply by the cell volume (240 cells per side of the sampling box).

worked.answer: $9\pi/4\approx7.0686$; the sampled value 7.0684 agrees to 3e-4 relative. The sampling needs only the sign of the field, which is the whole advantage of the SDF for Booleans. Analytic and numerical results computed and checked with scripts.

analyze.q: A fillet of radius $r$ is requested on a concave inside corner of an SDF solid. Why does the 'shrink by $r$, grow by $r$' trick round convex corners but not concave ones, and what is the fix?
analyze.hint: Think of a ball of radius $r$ rolling inside versus outside the solid.

analyze.q: Why is the intersection of two exact SDFs not an exact SDF outside the solid, yet the rendered surface is still correct?
analyze.hint: What does the zero level set depend on, and what does ray marching need beyond it?

analyze.q: Two B-rep faces that should meet along an edge are 1e-6 apart. List what the kernel must decide, and what can go wrong in a later Boolean.
analyze.hint: Tolerance, edge sharing, topology of the result.

evaluate.q: You need to model a lattice of thousands of struts for additive manufacture. Which representation would you choose, and what do you lose?
evaluate.hint: Cost of Booleans versus exact CAD features.

evaluate.hint: Where are the bad cells, and what does the solver do there?

create: Build a bracket from a box and two cylindrical holes, first as an SDF using min and max, then list the B-rep faces, edges and vertices of the result and check the Euler formula.
Choose a smoothing parameter $k$ for a union of two spheres of radius 1 centred 1.5 apart so the neck has a visible fillet of about 0.2. How would you tune it, and how would you check the result?

checks.q: Why is union a minimum for signed distance functions?
checks.answer: A point is inside the union if it is inside either shape, that is if either distance is negative. The smaller of the two numbers is negative whenever either is, so $\min(f_A,f_B)<0$ exactly on the union. Its zero level set is the union's boundary.

checks.q: Find the volume of the solid made by revolving the disc $(x-3)^2+y^2\le1$ about the $y$-axis.
checks.answer: The area is $\pi$ and the centroid is at distance 3 from the axis, so $V=2\pi\cdot3\cdot\pi=6\pi^2\approx59.2$, the Studio's torus preset.

checks.q: A 2D mesh of $n=100$ points has $h=20$ on the convex hull and is Delaunay. How many triangles does it have, and how many edges?
checks.hint: $T=2n-2-h$, then Euler's formula for the planar graph.
checks.answer: $T=200-2-20=178$ triangles. Edges: $E=(3T+h)/2=(534+20)/2=277$. The Euler check $V-E+F=n-277+(178+1)=2$ confirms the counts.

checks.q: A team says their SDF-based union is exact, so no mesh cleaning is needed. What would you check before accepting that?
checks.hint: Exact where, and what comes after the SDF?
checks.answer: The min is exact only outside the union, and the surface must still be extracted by sampling the field on a grid, which introduces its own error and can create thin sliver triangles. Check the extraction resolution, that features smaller than a cell survive, and the quality of the extracted mesh before using it.

checks.q: Describe how you would make a part with a rounded rectangular slot using only SDF primitives.
checks.answer: Make the part as a box SDF. Make the slot as a rounded box, $f_\mathrm{box}(\mathbf b-r)-r$, with the slot's half-sizes and corner radius $r$. Take the difference $\max(f_\mathrm{part},-f_\mathrm{slot})$. Extract the zero level set to mesh, or sample the sign to voxelise.

Checked with sympy and numerically: SDF gradient, box SDF against brute force, min/max exactness, smooth-min limit, rounded-box corner, Pappus torus, sphere-union volume (analytic and grid), Euler counts, Delaunay emptiness and triangle count, element quality.
